newsitem.title: USA: INTERVIEW - Paxar sees rising revenues.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Paxar sees rising revenues.

text.p: Through acquisitions and expansion in Latin America and Asia, Paxar Corp Chief Executive Arthur Executive Arthur Hershaft said he sees the company as a billion-dollar-a-year venture within five years.
Paxar, which manufactures tags and labels for apparel clients worldwide, expects revenues of $500 million for 1997, Hershaft said in an interview.
For all of 1996, Paxar reported revenues of $219.8 million, up from $201.4 million in 1995.
On March 3 Paxar increased its stake in bar code company Monarch Marking Systems Inc from 49 percent to 100 percent for a price of $130 million.

"On an aperational level, we expect the deal to be neither accretive nor dilutive this year," Hershaft said in a recent interview with Reuters. "But this acquisition all of a sudden gets us onto some screens that we were not on before."

Monarch bar codes mark everything from spatulas to cans of beans on store shelves. Recently it grew to include wholesale packaging identification and tracking, or, put more simply, the business of printing the right label to go on the right box to make sure it gets shipped to the right store.
"The synergy is that almost everything that happens in the way of identification, price marking and tracking, you can now get from one source," Hershaft said.
Paxar has 30 percent of the U.S. apparel identification market and about four percent outside the U.S., Hershaft said, or about 15 percent of the combined world market.

In January the company acquired a 70 percent stake in Label Systems Industria Comercio Importacao Exportacao Ltda, now called Paxar do Brasil Ltda, in Santa Catarina, Brazil. The company said it does not expect the acquisition to be accretive this year.

Paxar has eight manufacturing sites in the U.S. and plants in Ancarano and Carpi, both in Italy; Nottingham and Runcorn, both in England; Warsaw, Poland; and Hong Kong. Monarch has manufacturing operations at its headquarters in Miamisburg, Ohio, and six other sites throughout the world.
Hershaft said international sales are increasing about 20 percent per year. He said he wants to grow them from their current 40 percent of overall business to 50 percent.
Hershaft said he expects 1997 capital spending excluding Monarch to be slightly less than last year's $13.8 million, and about $22 million including Monarch's operations.

He said Paxar is in talks to buy the privately held Golden State Group of Cos of Taiwan, as part of Hershaft's plan to make Paxar's product line as available in Asia and Latin America as it is in North America and Europe.

"It's surprising how unknown the company is," said analyst Walter Glazer with the firm of Wheat First Butcher Singer. "They don't really fit within any known industry group and people don't really know what to make of them."
Glazer said betting on Paxar is the same as betting on Hershaft.
"I wouldn't want to compete against him," Glazer said. "He's a guy with vision."
